anchor: {verificationId, architectureVersion, subject:commit:abc123, result, checks, evidence, findings} — a durable artifact. ArchitectureVersion → AssuranceRun → CheckResult → Evidence → Verification → {evaluates→ArchitectureRule, produces→Finding} — fits the KnowledgeOS graph model.
statement: Defines the machine-readable assurance-output schema and its relationship representation in the graph, enabling queries like 'which architectural rules are currently failing' or 'which exceptions permit current violations' — 'much more useful than a static architecture diagram.'

anchor: Contexts 7 PASS, Dependencies 128 PASS, Contracts 19 PASS, Architecture Rules 42 PASS, Warnings 3, Blocking Findings 0, Exceptions 2 — the UI is only a projection; assurance data remains authoritative elsewhere.
statement: Sketches an architecture-assurance dashboard example, restating that any UI over this data is a projection, not the authority.

anchor: Agent asks 'is my implementation architecturally valid?' and receives Architecture:PASS/Relevant findings:none/Applicable rules:7/Evidence:7 verification records, making its own workflow more deterministic. On failure, Finding+Reason+Suggested remediation lets the agent modify code and rerun assurance — a self-correcting architecture loop.
statement: Presents agent-facing self-assurance query/response and the self-correcting loop (Agent->Modify->Architecture Assurance->{PASS, FAIL->Finding->Agent}), called 'one of the strongest practical uses of KnowledgeOS'; states the architecture thereby becomes an 'Executable Constraint System,' no longer a static diagram.

anchor: ASSURE-001: Every blocking architecture rule has an executable checker. ASSURE-002: Every checker declares whether it is deterministic. ASSURE-003: Every completed assurance run produces traceable evidence. ASSURE-004: Architecture findings reference the exact rule and architecture version. ASSURE-005: Blocking findings cannot be silently suppressed. ASSURE-006: Approved exceptions are explicit, scoped and time-bounded where required. ASSURE-007: Runtime-critical invariants have behavioral contract tests.
statement: Defines seven Self-Assurance Engine invariants ASSURE-001..007.

anchor: MachineAssurance ≠ CompleteArchitectureGovernance. Machine→Observe→Check→Produce Finding→Human Governance→Decision. AI→Analyze Finding→Propose Remediation→Human/Governance→Approve where required.
statement: States the Self-Assurance Engine's important limitation — some architectural properties remain qualitative/organizational/contextual/governance-dependent, requiring human judgment — and gives the human-decision-boundary and AI-decision-boundary diagrams: the machine must not silently transform a technical finding into a governance decision, and AI can accelerate but not replace governance.

anchor: ArchitectureRule → Checker → Evidence → Verification, the same mechanism used to verify the mechanism itself. KnowledgeOS governs engineering and governs itself, but bounded to Architecture→Implementation→Runtime to avoid infinite meta-layers.
statement: States the recursive property that KnowledgeOS concepts govern KnowledgeOS itself, with an explicit bound against infinite meta-layering.

anchor: KnowledgeOS architecture can become machine-checkable, evidence-producing, and continuously verifiable. Constitution→Registry→Implementation→Runtime→Observation→Evidence→Verification→Finding→Governance.
statement: Step 154 verdict boxing the core property established across Steps 152-154 and the complete governance-assurance chain, including the complete self-assurance loop diagram (Constitution->Registry->Self-Assurance Engine->{Registry,Static,Runtime Checks}->Evidence->Verification->{PASS,FAIL->Finding->Governance->Exception->Registry Update}).

anchor: Who is allowed to change the architecture, the rules, the Registry, and the enforcement mechanisms themselves? Machine verifies conformance; Governance decides what architecture should be.
statement: Opens Step 155 (KnowledgeOS Governance Runtime): the most important organizational question, previewing the architecture-change lifecycle (Architecture Change->Proposal->Impact Analysis->Architecture Review->Decision->Registry Version->Implementation->Assurance->Effective Architecture) connecting the technical assurance model back to Architecture Board/Domain Architect/Governance responsibilities, with the crucial machine-verifies-vs-governance-decides distinction.

anchor: Governance decides. Assurance verifies. Engineering implements. AI assists.
statement: States the foundational four-way separation as one of the strongest invariants of KnowledgeOS; defines the Governance Runtime's responsibility (architecture changes, rule changes, exceptions, approvals, effective versions, accountability, decision records) as distinct from performing technical verification itself, with the governance architecture pipeline Change Proposal->Impact Analysis->Architecture Review->Governance Decision->{REJECT, APPROVE->Registry Version->Implementation->Assurance->{PASS,FAIL}} — 'approval precedes effectiveness, while assurance follows implementation.'

anchor: Proposal ≠ Decision ≠ Implementation(Observation) ≠ Verification — four distinct domain concepts, not sequential statuses of one object.
statement: States the four-question model (what is proposed / what has been approved / what has actually been implemented / does implementation conform) and works four pairwise non-equivalences: Proposal ≠ Decision (an AI proposal to introduce a bounded context is not an ArchitectureDecision); Decision ≠ Implementation (Board approval ≠ code already changed); Implementation ≠ Conformance (only assurance establishes Conformant); Conformance ≠ Approval (code can technically conform to an unapproved architecture) — 'this distinction is extremely important.'

anchor: PROPOSED → APPROVED → IMPLEMENTED → VERIFIED — not sequential statuses of one object, but belonging to Proposal/Decision/Implementation/Verification respectively.
statement: Defines the GovernanceDecision aggregate (states DRAFT/SUBMITTED/UNDER_REVIEW/APPROVED/REJECTED/SUPERSEDED, lifecycle organization-defined) and the Architecture Change Proposal schema (proposalId, subject, requestedChange, rationale, affectedArchitecture, impactAssessment, proposer, status), noting the proposal itself is not authoritative architecture.

anchor: AI-assisted impact analysis (Registry, repository, dependency graph, historical decisions, existing evidence) remains ImpactAssessment=Analysis, not a governance decision. Deterministic impact analysis (e.g. 'remove Module B' -> checker identifies 17 dependent modules) is strong evidence the AI can explain.
statement: Defines impact-analysis scope (Bounded Contexts, Dependencies, APIs, Events, Persistence, Security, Operations, Teams, Processes, Existing Exceptions) partly automated and distinguishes AI-generated impact summaries (still analysis, not decision) from deterministic impact checks (strong evidence).

anchor: Actor ≠ Authority — e.g. Actor: Domain Architect, Authority: Architecture Board.
statement: Requires the Registry to identify the responsible authority per decision type (e.g. Architecture Principle Change->Architecture Board, Implementation Exception->designated approval authority), coming from the organization's actual governance model rather than being invented; distinguishes the person performing an operation (Actor) from the empowered organizational role/body (Authority).

anchor: Decision D42 basedOn ImpactAssessment, basedOn ArchitectureEvidence, basedOn RiskAssessment, produces ApprovedArchitectureVersion — decision traceability. Architecture Version → Decision → Proposal → Impact Analysis → Evidence → Original Observations — governed architectural memory.
statement: Requires a decision to reference its supporting evidence and defines the full provenance traversal answering 'why was this architecture approved,' called 'governed architectural memory.'

anchor: Architecture v1.1 Status=APPROVED, Effective=2026-10-01. Before that date, v1.0 may remain applicable. ApplicableArchitecture = f(date, effectiveVersions, exceptions). A September-15 release must be evaluated against v1.0, not v1.1.
statement: Formalizes temporal governance Architecture(t) with a worked historical-verification example showing which version applies to a release depending on effective dates, essential for correct historical audit; requires supersession (v1.0-supersededBy->v1.1) to keep v1.0 historically available, never overwritten; states approved decisions are historical — corrections produce new records rather than editing the original.

anchor: ProposalSubmitted, ReviewStarted, ImpactAssessmentCompleted, DecisionApproved, DecisionRejected, ArchitectureVersionApproved, ArchitectureVersionActivated, ArchitectureVersionSuperseded, ExceptionApproved, ExceptionExpired.
statement: Lists a candidate ten-event governance vocabulary, to be derived from the actual lifecycle.

anchor: Exception ≠ ArchitectureChange — approving that Module X may temporarily violate Rule R does not mean Rule R has changed. Exception{exceptionId,ruleId,subject,scope,rationale,approver,approvedAt,effectiveFrom,expiresAt,conditions}. Conditions prevent a blanket bypass.
statement: Elaborates the exception mechanism (Architecture Rule->Violation->Exception Request->Governance Decision->{REJECT->violation remains blocking, APPROVE->constrained deviation}), the exception schema, and worked conditional examples (e.g. allowed only if module remains isolated, no production deployment, migration completed by date X).

anchor: Governance Runtime defines Applicable Architecture → Assurance Engine verifies → Implementation; Assurance Finding flows back to Governance Runtime. GOVERNANCE → Architecture Rule → IMPLEMENTATION → ASSURANCE → {PASS, FAIL→FINDING→GOVERNANCE}.
statement: Presents the Governance Runtime/Assurance Engine interaction and the resulting operational governance feedback loop.

anchor: Governance must not consume only AI summaries ('the proposed change affects three contexts'); the authoritative basis is Evidence+Impact Assessment+Architecture Registry+Existing Decisions+Risk Information, with the AI explanation only a convenience layer.
statement: States governance decisions must rest on traceable evidence, not AI-generated summaries alone.

anchor: Context service reused for Developer→Engineering Context, Agent→Agent Context, Domain Architect→Architecture Context, Architecture Board→Governance Context. Context = f(Subject,Task,Role,Authority,Scope).
statement: Extends the Context Service to serve governance users (Architecture Board member context: Proposal, Current/Proposed Architecture, Impact, Findings, Exceptions, Evidence, Previous Decisions) and generalizes Context as role-sensitive — a powerful reuse of the platform across all actor types.
